Active Membrane Transport • Important carrier protein in human cells • Sodium-potassium pump (Na + /K + ATPase) • Most studied pump • Pumps 3 Na + out of cell and 2 K + back into cell • Present in all plasma membranes, but especially active in nerve cells and muscle cells

Active Membrane Transport • Endocytosis • Involves formation of vesicles by invagination of cell membrane to transport certain substance into cytoplasm • Example: Phagocytosis • The cell engulfs a large particle by enclosing it within a vesicle called a phagosome. The phagosome is then combined with a lysosome.

Active Membrane Transport • Exocytosis • Process where material is ejected from cell by secretory vesicle • Secretory vesicle contains the molecules. The vesicle fuses with cell membrane and release the molecules to outside of cell. ○ Examples ■ hormones, neurotransmitters, mucus, cellular wastes

Revision: Structure and Properties of Cell Membrane
• Cell membrane
• Phospholipid bilayer
• Functions
• Separate intracellular region and extracellular region
• Control substances entering and exiting the cell
• Property
• Selective permeability
• Cell membrane allows some substances to pass in different rates while it restricts certain other substances to pass

Selective permeability of cell membrane
(1)Small non-polar molecules pass the phospholipid bilayer quickly
(2)Polar molecules or ions need to use certain transporter proteins (channel proteins or carrier
proteins) to pass cell membrane
(3)Big molecules (or large amount of substance at the same time) need to form vesicles to pass cell
membrane

Membrane Transport and Membrane Potential
• Selective permeability of cell membrane leads to different concentrations of charged particles in cytoplasm and in extracellular fluid. This results in membrane potential, the difference of voltage across the cell membrane.
• In resting state, resting membrane potentials of all human cells range from - 50mV to -100mV, depending on cell type.
• negative sign (-) indicates inside of cell is more negative than outside of cell

Active Membrane Transport
• Two major types of active membrane transport methods
• Active transport
• Vesicular transport
• Both require cellular energy to move molecules across plasma membrane for any of these reasons:
• Molecule is too large for channel proteins
• Molecule is not lipid soluble
• Molecule is not able to move down concentration gradient

Active Membrane Transport
• Active Transport
• Requires special carrier proteins (pumps )
• Moves molecules against their concentration gradient (from low to high) ○ This requires energy directly or indirectly ○ Some pumps transport more than one substance
• Antiporters
• transport one substance into cell while transporting a different substance out of cell
• Symporters
• transport two different substances in the same direction

Active Membrane Transport
• Two types of active transport:
• Primary active transport
• Required energy directly
• Secondary active transport
• Required energy indirectly from ionic gradients created by primary active transport

Passive Membrane Transport
• Facilitated diffusion
• Certain polar water-soluble molecules (e.g. glucose, amino acids, and ions) are transported passively down their concentration gradient by:
• Carrier-mediated facilitated diffusion
• Substances bind to carrier proteins
• E.g. glucose, amino acids
• Channel-mediated facilitated diffusion
• Substances move through channel proteins
• E.g. calcium ions, sodium ions, potassium ions

Membrane Transport and Membrane Potential
• Generation and Maintaining of Resting Membrane Potential
• (1) Proteins with negative charge are too large and polar. They cannot pass across cell membrane and will be trapped inside cell.
• (2) Cell membrane is somehow more permeable to K +. K + are transported out of cells by facilitated diffusion.
• (3) Action of Na + /K + pump brings more ions with positive charge out of cell.
• Change of membrane potential is very important for the function of mus
